That fidelity is B's selling point. ::: {.callout-warning} ## B's fragility — each invariant breaks silently if violated B works only because several fragile things are exactly right: the signal is keyed on the inherited `pid` (key it on `get_name(env)` and the companion signals nobody); the patient treats via a *registry event*, not in the trap handler (otherwise the competing risks are not resampled); the companion carries **no** state tally (otherwise the clone double-counts or double-releases it); and leaving `S1` must `send()` an abandon signal so a still-queued companion reneges out. Get any one wrong and the model produces plausible-looking but wrong numbers. Approach A has none of these failure modes — which is the whole tradeoff, and the subject of Part IV. ::: # Part IV — The swing, and which model to trust We now have four readings of the same decision, differing only in how seriously they take the confirmatory bottleneck. Lined up, they tell the story the whole document was built to tell. ## The cost-effectiveness drift: SE → SW ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Re-run the field-minus-molecular increment under each treatment of the queue. incr <- function(model_file, N = 2000, seed = 7) { source(here::here("R", model_file), chdir = TRUE) # each redefines des_run() cleanly arm <- function(s) des_run(modifyList(inputs, list(strategy = s, N = N)), seed = seed) |> group_by(name) |> summarise(c = sum(dcost), q = sum(dqaly), .groups = "drop") |> summarise(c = mean(c), q = mean(q)) m <- arm("mol"); f <- arm("field") c(dcost = f$c - m$c, dqaly = f$q - m$q) } drift <- rbind( `8 — no queue` = incr("model-8.R"), `9 — exogenous wait` = incr("model-9.R"), `10 — endogenous (A)` = incr("model10.R"), `11 — endogenous (B)` = incr("model11.R")) ## Molecular : dcost = 3075 dQALY = 11.656 ## Field : dcost = 3043 dQALY = 11.905 ## Δcost = -32 ΔdQALY = 0.249 ## SE quadrant: field test is dominant (lower cost, more QALYs) ## Molecular (exog queue): dcost = 3063 dQALY = 11.621 ## Field (exog queue): dcost = 3040 dQALY = 11.910 ## Δcost = -23 ΔdQALY = 0.289 ## Quadrant: SE (dominant) ## Molecular (endog queue, A): dcost = 3079 dQALY = 11.565 ## Field (endog queue, A): dcost = 2989 dQALY = 11.598 ## Δcost = -91 ΔdQALY = 0.032 ## Quadrant: SE (dominant) ## Molecular (FIFO companion, B): dcost = 3060 dQALY = 11.601 ## Field (FIFO companion, B): dcost = 3005 dQALY = 11.565 ## Δcost = -55 ΔdQALY = -0.037 ## Quadrant: SW quad <- ifelse(drift[,"dcost"] < 0 & drift[,"dqaly"] > 0, "SE (dominant)", ifelse(drift[,"dcost"] < 0 & drift[,"dqaly"] < 0, "SW (cheaper, worse)", "other")) knitr::kable( data.frame(`Δ cost` = round(drift[,"dcost"]), `Δ QALY` = round(drift[,"dqaly"], 3), Quadrant = quad, check.names = FALSE), caption = "The same field-vs-molecular decision, under four treatments of the confirmatory queue.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The same field-vs-molecular decision, under four treatments of the confirmatory queue. | | Δ cost| Δ QALY|Quadrant | |:-------------------|------:|------:|:-------------------| |8 — no queue | -29| 0.261|SE (dominant) | |9 — exogenous wait | -24| 0.267|SE (dominant) | |10 — endogenous (A) | -52| -0.016|SW (cheaper, worse) | |11 — endogenous (B) | -48| -0.020|SW (cheaper, worse) | ::: ::: Read the `Δ QALY` column top to bottom: **+0.26 → +0.27 → −0.02 → −0.02**. The cost column never changes sign — the field test is cheaper in every row, because its cost advantage is the *test*, and the queue does not touch that. What the queue moves is the **health** axis, and it moves it across zero. Ignoring capacity, or modelling it exogenously, the field test is **dominant** (southeast): an easy yes. Model the bottleneck *endogenously* — by either design — and the same field test lands in the **southwest**: still cheaper, but now *worse* for health, because the referrals it generates overwhelm the confirmatory capacity and its extra cancers progress untreated in the line. The recommendation does not merely weaken; it **flips quadrant**. A decision-maker who saw only Models 8–9 would adopt the field test as a free win. A decision-maker who saw Models 10–11 faces a genuine trade-off: real savings bought with real health loss — the "southwest-quadrant quandary." ## Approach A vs B: where they agree, and where they part The two endogenous designs agreed in the table above. Do they agree in general? We compared them by **replication** — not by shared seeds. (Common random numbers align the two *strategies* within one model, but they cannot align two *different* models: A and B inject different confirm-handling events into the loop, so the reactive resample consumes the disease draws at different cadences. Pairing A against B on a shared seed measures that cadence artifact, not the models. So we run each model over many independent cohorts and compare the means.) ::: {.callout-note} ## A = B on the bottom line, with a caveat (30 independent replications) Over 30 independent cohorts (`validation/validate-AB-replication.R`), A and B **agree on the cost axis**: the field test is cheaper by ≈ \$47/person under both, well within Monte-Carlo error. On the **health axis** they sit a hair apart and on opposite sides of zero: Approach B (the exact queue) puts the incremental QALY at about **−0.04** (southwest), while Approach A (the analytic wait) puts it at about **0.00** — right on the SE/SW boundary. The gap is small and not statistically sharp at 30 reps, but it is *directional*: A's M/M/c wait is a touch optimistic under heavy saturation, so it under-states the health loss exactly where the decision is closest. The convenient model and the faithful model can land on opposite sides of the line precisely where it matters most. ::: ### The tradeoff, stated plainly So which to use? It depends on the regime, and the table is the guide: - **Mild contention** (the queue rarely binds): A and B agree to within noise. Prefer **A** — it adds the queue with one resource and two registry events, never edits the engine, and has none of B's fragile signal-and-clone machinery. - **Heavy contention** (the queue saturates — exactly the policy-relevant case here, where a cheap test floods a fixed capacity): A's analytic wait drifts optimistic. Prefer **B** — its queue is the exact emergent FIFO, and when the recommendation sits on the SE/SW boundary you want the model that does not approximate the very thing the decision hinges on. B is the **defensible** choice for a real recommendation; A is the fast, transparent check that tells you whether contention matters at all before you pay for B. ## What the decision looks like For the Republic of SMDM, the analysis does not hand back a verdict; it hands back the *shape* of the choice. The field test is genuinely cheaper and genuinely reaches more women — but only if the confirmatory pathway can absorb what it sends. As modelled, it cannot: the bottleneck converts reach into waiting, and waiting into progression. The lever that decides the outcome is therefore not the test at all — it is **capacity**. Adopting the field test *and* expanding confirmatory throughput could keep it in the southeast; adopting it alone moves it to the southwest. That coupling — between a screening choice and a downstream resource — is invisible to a model that treats confirmation as instantaneous or its wait as fixed, and it is the entire reason to reach for discrete-event simulation here. ## Limitations and honest extensions This is a deliberately spare, generic model; several real features are omitted, each of which would deepen (not reverse) the story: - **False-positive harms are costs only, not health.** A false positive here pays for a test and a workup and consumes a slot, but suffers no anxiety, procedure risk, or disutility. The field test's heavy false-positive burden would look worse, not better, with those on the health axis. - **No overdiagnosis.** Every detected `S1` case here would have progressed; none is indolent disease that screening finds and treats needlessly. Overdiagnosis is a central screening harm and would further penalise the higher-coverage test. - **One bottleneck, not two.** Only confirmation is capacity-constrained; oncology treatment is assumed available on demand. Real systems queue there too. - **Loss-to-follow-up is folded into progression.** Patients leave the queue only by progressing, recovering, or dying — not by disengaging after a long wait, which in the case study falls hardest on the rural women the expansion is meant to reach. An explicit dropout hazard is the natural next event to add. - **Constant hazards, no age structure; a single lumped advanced state.** Standard simplifications for a teaching model; none is load-bearing for the SE→SW result. Each of these three is a place where careful, reasonable code is silently wrong. ::: {.callout-important} ## `send()` is global; a queued arrival is deaf to it anyway These two facts compound. First, there is **no per-arrival signal channel** in `simmer` — `send("x")` wakes *every* arrival currently in `trap("x")` / `wait()`. The only way to address one patient is to encode the patient id into the signal *string* (`paste0("acq_", pid)`), and a typo or attribute mismatch in that string is dropped without any error. Second, and worse for the naive fix, an arrival that is **blocked inside `seize()` does not process `trap()`/`wait()` at all** — the signal machinery is suspended for the duration of the block. So the one patient you most want to reach (the one stuck in the queue) is precisely the one a broadcast cannot wake. This is why Approach B never lets the *patient* block: only the disposable companion sits in the `seize` queue, and it is reachable via `renege_if`, not `trap`. ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Clones carry attribute *values*, not the seize *ledger* `clone()` is not a deep copy of process state. The children share a snapshot of attribute values, but each maintains its **own, private record of which resources it currently holds**. A resource seized *before* the `clone()` therefore sits in an ambiguous place: each child believes it can release it, but the underlying server count can only be decremented once. The second release underflows the count and `simmer` aborts mid-run (`'' not previously seized`). Because the offending release happens at an RNG-dependent moment, the crash looks *intermittent* — the most expensive kind of bug to chase. The discipline that follows (and that Approach B obeys): **never seize a shared tally on the patient before cloning, and never let a clone touch the state counters at all.** B's companion touches only the contended `confirm` resource; the patient touches only its tallies. The clone boundary is also a resource boundary, so no ledger is ever redeemed twice. ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Live occupancy is readable from inside a `time_to_event` sampler This is the single permissive fact the whole of Approach A turns on, and it is easy to assume is forbidden. A `time_to_event` function in the event registry is just an R closure evaluated when the engine reschedules; nothing stops it from calling `get_server_count(env, "confirm")` and `get_capacity(env, "confirm")` on a *real* finite resource. So congestion can be read at sampling time and converted directly into a wait — longer when more slots are busy and more patients sit ahead in the FIFO position — with the patient never entering a blocking `seize`. The cap is then enforced *separately*, at fire time, by a guard that performs the real `seize` only when `get_server_count < get_capacity`. The wait is an analytic M/M/c-flavoured approximation (correct mean under saturation); the capacity is exact. Instead, each patient owns a **private bank** of uniforms, drawn once from a deterministic per-patient seed, and every stochastic step consumes the bank by inverse-CDF (`qexp(u, rate)` for `rexp`, `u < p` for `runif`). Because the bank is private and fixed, two *strategies* hand patient *i* identical draws; patient *i*'s disease is bit-for-bit the same in both arms until the screening *decision* diverges, so the paired difference is the decision's effect with the cohort noise differenced away. The helpers `draw_exp()` / `draw_unif()` fall back to plain `rexp` / `runif` when no bank is armed, which is why Models 1–6 are unchanged to the last digit. **The hard limit.** CRN aligns two *strategies within one model*. It **cannot** align two *different models* — Approach A and Approach B inject different confirm-handling events into the loop, so the reactive resample consumes each patient's disease bank at a different *cadence*, and the same seed yields different draws. A shared-seed A-vs-B comparison therefore measures that cadence artifact, not the models; we even see A ≠ B under a *null-effect* run, where the queue is inert. So A-vs-B agreement must be established by **independent replication** (Part IV), not by CRN — a subtle but load-bearing distinction when the two models are being compared head-to-head. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A practical gotcha in the banks The per-patient seed is `CRN$seed + patient_index`, so two runs whose seeds differ by less than the cohort size draw **overlapping** banks — their "independent" cohorts are nearly identical. For genuinely independent replications (e.g. the variance demo in Model 8, or the A-vs-B harness), space the run seeds widely (`seed * 123457`), not by consecutive integers. :::
